rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gave Muhammad a decisive refutation of shirk suited to his place as final messenger; earlier messengers instead sought God's judgment after rejection.
rows.anchor: اختصاصا لم يلقنه من سبق من الرسل

rows.speaker: الرسول
rows.claim: At the Farewell Pilgrimage sermon, the Prophet said Satan despaired of being worshipped in Arabia but accepted lesser acts of obedience people deem trivial.
rows.anchor: إن الشيطان قد يئس أن يعبد في أرضكم هذه ولكنه قد رضي أن يطاع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A messenger comes from the people's own kind so they can interact; if angels inhabited earth, an angel would be sent, whereas humans receive a human messenger.
rows.anchor: أن الله يرسل الرسول للقوم من نوعهم للتمكين من المخالطة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Walking” describes the angels; “settled” is circumstantial and means firmly dwelling on earth rather than temporarily arriving on a mission.
rows.anchor: وأريد به هنا المتمكن غير المضطرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since walking and settling on earth characterize humans, the point is that God sent humans a human messenger; messengers bring guidance by calling people to it.
rows.anchor: لو كنتم ملائكة لنزلنا عليكم من السماء ملكا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After teaching Muhammad a decisive argument, God also teaches the earlier prophets' appeal to Him as judge, consoling and strengthening him and promising judgment between him and his opponents.
rows.anchor: أردف ذلك بتلقينه أيضا ما لقنه الرسل السابقين من تفويض الأمر إلى الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appeal summarizes a response to all their preceding demands; the omitted object of “suffice” is “for me.”
rows.anchor: وفي هذا رد لمجموع مقترحاتهم المتقدمة على وجه الإجمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A witness is one who reports events as they occurred; here witness figuratively means helper and judge for the one in the right, because testimony leads to judgment.
rows.anchor: وأريد بالشهيد هنا الشهيد للمحق على المبطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prefixed bāʾ intensifies the verb's attachment to its subject; the underlying construction is that God suffices as witness.
rows.anchor: والباء الداخلة على اسم الجلالة زائدة لتأكيد لصوق فعل كفى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's knowledge explains why He suffices: He knows intentions and realities, and sees persons and their observable conditions comprehensively.
rows.anchor: وأريد به العليم بالنوايا والحقائق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The guidance clause may continue 17:94, combining ordinary visible obstacles with the real cause: God withholds enabling grace from those persisting in disbelief despite clear proof and following desire over reason.
rows.anchor: المانع الحقيقي وهو حرمان التوفيق من الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively it may continue 17:96 as further consolation: Muhammad need not grieve their failure, because God deprived them of guidance after their stubbornness preceded reflection on the message.
rows.anchor: أي لا يحزنك عدم اهتدائهم فإن الله حرمهم الاهتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance here means faith in what the Messenger brought.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالهدى الهدى إلى الإيمان بما جاء به الرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite form in “the guided” may refer to a mentally understood class, equaling the indefinite, and prepares for the contrast with those led astray.
rows.anchor: فائدة الإخبار عنه بأنه مهتد التوطئة إلى ذكر مقابله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the definite form restricts guidance to those God guides, against those Muhammad wishes to guide but God misguides; it cannot imply perfect guidance because faith-guidance is meant.
rows.anchor: يفيد قصر الهداية على الذي هداه الله قصرا إضافيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The written form drops the final yāʾ in keeping with pause pronunciation, an eloquent easing of the heavy participle ending in a weak consonant.
rows.anchor: لغة فصيحة غير جارية على القياس ولكنها أوثرت من جهة التخفيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr retain yāʾ in connected recitation and mark it finely in red; other readers drop it in liaison too, treating verse endings like poetic rhymes, as Sibawayh illustrates.
rows.anchor: قرأها نافع وأبو عمرو بإثبات الياء في الوصل وهو الوجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Addressing the Prophet for consolation, “you will not find helpers” denies their existence, since any existing helpers would be findable.
rows.anchor: فنفي وجدان الأولياء كناية عن نفي وجود الأولياء لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awliyāʾ can mean supporters who rescue them from punishment or guardians who could improve their condition and move them from misguidance.
rows.anchor: والأولياء : الأنصار ، أي لن تجد لهم أنصارا يخلصونهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural covers each person and the group collectively, as when it is said that a people rode their mounts.
rows.anchor: لن تجد لكل واحد وليا ولا لجماعته وليا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Besides Him” means someone other than God.
rows.anchor: ومن دونه } أي غيره .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The gathering collects people from scattered places; “on” their faces implies walking, and the Prophet answered that the One who made them walk on feet can make them walk on faces.
rows.anchor: والحشر : جمع الناس من مواضع متفرقة إلى مكان واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Walking on faces combines humiliation and pain because faces endure hard ground less well than feet; it reverses their portrayal of truth as error and error as truth.
rows.anchor: والمقصود من ذلك الجمع بين التشويه والتعذيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their faces replace their feet as walking limbs; blindness, muteness, and deafness punish false attacks on the Messenger and Qur'an and refusal to hear truth, and blindness at gathering deprives them of sight's pleasure.
rows.anchor: ثم كانوا { عميا وبكما } جزاء أقوالهم الباطلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The grotesque punishment prompts an explanatory answer: it recompenses disbelief in God's signs and denial of resurrection; “that” points to the preceding punishment.
rows.anchor: استئناف بياني لأن العقاب الفظيع المحكي يثير في نفوس السامعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Recompense is compensation for a deed; the bāʾ in “because they” marks causation.
rows.anchor: والجزاء : العوض عن عمل . والباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two causes are given: denial of the signs suits face-first gathering and sensory deprivation; denial of resurrection suits punishment for rejecting renewed life after decay.
rows.anchor: وذكر سببان : أحدهما : الكفر بالآيات ويندرج فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The questions about resurrection are rhetorical denials; charred remains would be more utterly diminished than bones decayed in soil.
rows.anchor: والاستفهام في حكاية قولهم : { أإذا كنا عظاما } وقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers differed over retaining the two hamzas in the questions, as at a parallel passage in this surah.
rows.anchor: وتقدم اختلاف القراء في إثبات الهمزتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After threatening the deniers, the verse refutes them by analogy: creating heaven and earth from nonbeing is greater than recreating decayed bodies.
rows.anchor: عطف عليه إبطال اعتقادهم بطريق الاستدلال بقياس التمثيل في الإمكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative rebukes and expresses amazement at their failure to know; their denial makes them seem unaware of God's proofs, although they know in reality.
rows.anchor: مشوب بتعجيب من انتفاء علمهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeing means believing or knowing, since God's ability to create is not visible; “them” refers to the idolaters called people in 17:94.
rows.anchor: والرؤية مستعملة في الاعتقاد لأنها عديت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Their like” can mean similar people, implying new bodies modeled on earthly bodies receive the same spirits; this hints that resurrection creates new bodies from nothing, not identical particles.
rows.anchor: قادر على أن يخلق ناسا أمثالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “like” figuratively means the referent itself, so God can recreate them, no more extraordinarily than creating heaven and earth.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون لفظ مثل هنا كناية عن نفس ما أضيف إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars offer three accounts of resurrection: re-creation from nothing, reassembly of dispersed parts, or a new analogous body growing from each person's coccyx as a tree grows from its seed.
rows.anchor: ولعلمائنا طرق في إعادة الأجسام عند البعث فقيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God the One who created heaven and earth points to an acknowledged, observable act of creation underlying the argument.
rows.anchor: ووصف اسم الجلالة بالموصول للإيماء إلى وجه بناء الخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The appointed term may be the resurrection time fixed in God's knowledge; humans are singled out because they deny it, though it includes everyone.
rows.anchor: والأجل هنا محتمل لإرادة الوقت الذي جعل لوقوع البعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this reading, “no doubt” means there should be no doubt; doubters are obstinate or avert themselves from reflection, as in 2:2.
rows.anchor: ريب المرتابين فيه مكابرة أو إعراض عن النظر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the term is their lifespan, a second proof of resurrection: God gave them life and an endpoint so He can restore them to a greater, lasting life.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون الأجل أجل الحياة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the term means lifespan, its certainty is evident; mentioning it alludes to the favor of respite and sustenance during life.
rows.anchor: تعريضا بالمنة بنعمة الإمهال على كلا المعنيين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The wrongdoers refused all but ingratitude” follows from their knowing God's power and still rejecting it, heightening rebuke and amazement.
rows.anchor: وجملة { فأبى الظالمون إلا كفورا } تفريع على الجملتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception of ingratitude reinforces refusal with what sounds like its opposite; kufūr means thankless denial of required belief and worship of someone other than the benefactor.
rows.anchor: واستثناء الكفور من الإباية تأكيد للشيء بما يشبه ضده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present tense supposes future possession; “withheld” functions intransitively for becoming miserly, without any particular object.
rows.anchor: واختير الفعل المضارع لأن المقصود فرض أن يملكوا ذلك في المستقبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding idhan to the conditional answer strengthens its response and conveys recompense, as at 17:42; Bishr ibn ʿAwanah's poetry illustrates the particle.
rows.anchor: وأكد جواب ( لو ) بزيادة حرف ( إذن ) فيه لتقوية معنى الجوابية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about human miserliness is parenthetical or circumstantial and a general coda, so its wāw does not coordinate it.
rows.anchor: وجملة وكان الإنسان قتورا } حالية أو اعتراضية في آخر الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qatūr means intensely stingy and derives from qatr, constriction in spending.
rows.anchor: مشتق من القتر وهو التضييق في الإنفاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demand that the sky fall in fragments was not answered with the other proposals because it asks for a terrifying punishment sign, like Moses' nine signs.
rows.anchor: لأن له مخالفة لبقية ما اقترحوه بأنه اقتراح آية عذاب ورعب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' nine clear signs did not guide Pharaoh and his people, who called them magic; their case exemplifies obstinate rejecters such as Quraysh and consoles Muhammad.
rows.anchor: فلم يهتد فرعون وقومه وزعموا ذلك سحرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nine signs are the shining hand, serpent staff, flood, locusts, lice, frogs, blood, boils as the plague, and drought with crop loss, listed in al-Aʿrāf and summarized by al-Fīrūzābādī's verse.
rows.anchor: والآيات التسع هي : بياض يده كلما أدخلها في جيبه وأخرجها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs answer miracle demands; throughout the surah, comparing Muhammad's and Moses' missions argues against those rejecting a human messenger and People of the Book who supplied objections.
rows.anchor: ثم لم يزل الاعتناء في هذه السورة بالمقارنة بين رسالة محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs statement can coordinate either with “I am only a human messenger” or with the statement about God's treasures in 17:100.
rows.anchor: فتكون هذه الجملة عطفا على جملة قل سبحان ربي هل كنت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage turns to Israel as evidence against Quraysh and alludes to Israel's rejection of Muhammad and circulation of objections, recalling Pharaoh's accusation that Moses was bewitched.
rows.anchor: ثم انتقل من ذلك بطريقة التفريع إلى التسجيل ببني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ask the Children of Israel” addresses the Prophet and means to cite them as evidence against polytheists, not to seek information.
rows.anchor: والخطاب في قوله : { فسئل } للنبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's “bewitched” means afflicted by sorcery that spoiled Moses' reason and made him utter confused, false speech; this was said in a different exchange from other accusations.
rows.anchor: أي سحرك السحرة وأفسدوا عقلك فصرت تهرف بالكلام الباطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In that exchange Pharaoh focuses on Moses' strange utterances rather than the signs, as his appeal to the entourage, “Will you not listen?”, shows.
rows.anchor: ألا ترى إلى قوله تعالى حكاية عنه قال لمن حوله ألا تستمعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idh attaches to God's giving the signs; “they” in “when they came to them” means Israel, and the order is that Moses came to Israel, then they are asked.
rows.anchor: والضمير المنصوب في { جاءهم } عائد إلى بني إسرئيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh may have suspected either that the signs were magic or that Moses was bewitched; suspicion is weaker than certainty, though 45:32 shows ẓann can mean certain knowledge.
rows.anchor: وكان فرعون تعلق ظنه بحقيقة ما أظهر من الآيات فرجح عنده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh actually knew only God could send such signs; his accusation of sorcery was defiant arrogance and denial.
rows.anchor: أن تلك الآيات لا تكون إلا بتسخير الله إذ لا يقدر عليها غير الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' emphatic lām and qad assert Pharaoh's knowledge; Moses knew this by revelation or sound judgment, since necessary proof convinces an intact mind.
rows.anchor: وأكد كلام موسى بلام القسم وحرف التحقيق تحقيقا لحصول علم فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī alone reads “I knew,” taking Moses to deny that the signs were magic and express confidence that he was not bewitched.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الكسائي وحده { لقد علمت } بضم التاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “These” refers to the nine signs and uses a rational-person demonstrative, a familiar construction; Jarīr also uses أولئك for days.
rows.anchor: والإشارة ب { هؤلاء } إلى الآيات التسع جيء لها باسم إشارة العاقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baṣāʾir are proofs imparting inner sight, meaning knowledge; the phrase was explained at 7:203.
rows.anchor: والبصائر : الحجج المفيدة للبصيرة ، أي العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God the Lord of heaven and earth recalls that their Creator can produce such extraordinary signs.
rows.anchor: وعبر عن الله بطريق إضافة وصف الرب للسماوات والأرض تذكيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mathbūr means doomed to destruction and threatens Pharaoh with imminent ruin; Moses says “I think” from reverence, because he left a remote chance of repentance, or with certainty by usage.
rows.anchor: والمثبور : الذي أصابه الثبور وهو الهلاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Moses story completes comparison with Muhammad's opponents; Moses mirrors Pharaoh's wording to show fearlessness and answer him in kind.
rows.anchor: وجاء في جواب موسى عليه السلام لفرعون بمثل ما شافهه فرعون به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage returns to praising the Qur'an after 17:89 and objections from 17:90 onward; Pharaoh's denial creates the occasion for this return.
rows.anchor: عود إلى التنويه بشأن القرآن فهو متصل بقوله : { ولقد صرفنا للناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two clauses praise the Qur'an with distinct senses of truth: its sending is genuine and certain, answering denial of revelation; its arrival contains truth against falsehood and guidance for worldly and eternal welfare.
rows.anchor: فعلق إنزال الله إياه بأنه بالحق فكان معنى الحق الثابت الذي لا ريب فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronouns refer to the Qur'an; both bāʾs mark accompaniment because it includes truth and guidance, and their distinct senses prevent mere repetition.
rows.anchor: وضمائر الغيبة عائدة إلى القرآن المعروف من المقام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Preposing “in truth” in both clauses restricts the claim against those calling the Qur'an old tales, magic, or the like.
rows.anchor: وتقديم المجرور في الموضعين على عامله للقصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that Muhammad was sent only as bearer of good news and warning is parenthetical between the praise and 17:106.
rows.anchor: جملة معترضة بين جملة { وبالحق أنزلناه } وجملة { وقرآنا فرقناه }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Restricting the Prophet's mission to good news and warning answers those demanding divine acts from him and those who assumed a messenger could not be human.
rows.anchor: والقصر للرد على الذين سألوه أشياء من تصرفات الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse coordinates with 17:105; “Qur'an” is an advanced circumstantial phrase for the object pronoun, praising it as a recitable book whose name comes from recitation.
rows.anchor: عطف على جملة { أنزلناه ( الإسراء : 105 )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scripture has names—Book, Qur'an, Criterion, Reminder, Sending—used according to context; only Muhammad's revealed book is styled Qur'an.
rows.anchor: فهذا الكتاب له أسماء باختلاف صفاته فهو كتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faraqnāhu means divided it, revealing in portions rather than one mass; it may also mean clarified and distinguished it, so the phrase means divided and made it recitable.
rows.anchor: أي أنزلناه منجما مفرقا غير مجتمع صبرة واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its two purposes are reciting it to people and doing so slowly: the first explains its being a Qur'an, the second its piecemeal revelation, letting words and meanings settle in listeners.
rows.anchor: فهما علتان : أن يقرأ على الناس وتلك علة لجعله قرآنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubled verb and cognate object in “We sent it down” signal the gradual revelation already expressed by its division.
rows.anchor: وفي فعل { نزلناه } المضاعف وتأكيده بالمفعول المطلق إشارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The omitted wisdom is supplied by measured recitation and 25:32: gradual revelation strengthens the Prophet's heart.
rows.anchor: من اتحاد الحكمة . وهي ما صرح به قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, revelation was divided to accord with causes and events; both explanations answer those asking why it was not sent all at once.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يراد : فرقنا إنزاله رعيا للأسباب والحوادث

none: The segment contains only the recited text of verses 17:107-109.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address tells the Prophet to leave belief to Quraysh after arguments for the Qur'an's divine origin and merits, failed miracle demands, the witness of God, afterlife warning, Pharaoh's example, and gradual revelation.
rows.anchor: استئناف خطاب للنبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم ليلقنه بما يقوله للمشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Believe or do not believe” is an imperative of equal choice; lā is negation, not prohibition, conveying disregard and consolation as in 52:16.
rows.anchor: فالأمر في قوله : { آمنوا } للتسوية ، أي إن شئتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The learned people's faith explains this parity, the command, or both: scriptural knowers already believe the promised final Messenger, so Quraysh's faith is unnecessary.
rows.anchor: موقع ( إن ) فيها موقع فاء التفريع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling them learned indirectly calls those refusing the Qur'an ignorant and steeped in pre-Islamic ignorance.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا تعريض بأن الذين أعرضوا عن الإيمان بالقرآن جهلة وأهل جاهلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Examples include Waraqa ibn Nawfal, whose testimony was known in Mecca, and later converts ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām, Muʿayqīb, and Salmān al-Fārisī; this predicts the unseen.
rows.anchor: فقد تسامع أهل مكة بشهادته للنبيء صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronouns “in it,” “before it,” and “it is recited” refer to the Qur'an; context supplies omitted words meaning its truth and revelation.
rows.anchor: وضمائر ( به ، ومن قبله ، ويتلى ) عائدة إلى القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khurūr means falling, as in 16:26; the lām in “to the chins” means “on,” as in 37:103 and Taʾabbaṭa Sharran's line, whose phrase “ṣarīʿan lil-yadayni” witnesses the usage.
rows.anchor: واللام في للأذقان } بمعنى ( على ) كما في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām extends association into elevation, suggesting especially firm contact; adhqān are the lower jaw's joined point, and mention of chins conveys laying the whole face down eagerly.
rows.anchor: وأصل هذه اللام أنها استعارة تبعية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sujjadan is a circumstantial participle explaining that they fall in prostration to glorify God upon seeing proof of His knowledge, the messengers' truth, and His promise.
rows.anchor: وسجدا } جمع ساجد ، وهو في موضع الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Coordinating glorification with prostration joins bodily submission to verbal exaltation, as at 32:15; it expresses joy at the scriptural promise of the final Messenger.
rows.anchor: وعطفت { ويقولون سبحان ربنا } على { يخرون } للإشارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Our Lord's promise was fulfilled” completes their speech and is its central point: their earlier glorification expresses wonder at the promised book and Messenger.
rows.anchor: وجملة { إن كان وعد ربنا لمفعولا } من تمام مقولهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In is the lightened emphatic particle, followed commonly by a verb of the copula; the predicate lām distinguishes it from negative in.
rows.anchor: و ( إن ) مخففة من الثقيلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Promise retains its verbal-noun sense; its fulfillment entails that what was promised is realized, and mafulan means God brings it about.
rows.anchor: وتحقيق الوعد يستلزم تحقيق الموعود به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated falling scene is one prostration with weeping; repeating the clause with a changed circumstance emphasizes signs of reverence, as in the poet's repeated line.
rows.anchor: فالخرور المحكي بالجملة الثانية هو الخرور الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present tense of “weeping” makes the scene vivid; their tears express joy, though inward emotion can also arise from grief, fear, or yearning.
rows.anchor: وذكر { يبكون } بصيغة المضارع لاستحضار الحالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an increases their reverence beyond the awe they had from hearing their own scripture.
rows.anchor: ويزيدهم القرآن خشوعا على خشوعهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reciter and listener should prostrate at this verse in imitation of them; Muslims have even stronger reason to prostrate when Qur'an recounts such prostration.
rows.anchor: ومن السنة سجود القارىء والمستمع له بقصد هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The choice between Allah and al-Raḥmān has a specific occasion, since otherwise there is no reason to single this attribute out over other beautiful names.
rows.anchor: لا شك أن لنزول هذه الآية سببا خاصا إذ لا موجب لذكر هذا التخيير

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī and al-Wāḥidī report that the Prophet invoked “O Merciful, O Compassionate”; polytheists accused him of calling two gods, and the verse allowed either name, implicitly including al-Raḥīm.
rows.anchor: فأما سبب نزولها فروى الطبري والواحدي عن ابن عباس قال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf reports that Abū Jahl heard the Prophet say “O Allah, O Merciful” and accused him of invoking another deity; Ibn Mardawayh transmits it, and the author finds it more apt to the verse.
rows.anchor: وفي ( الكشاف ) : عن ابن عباس سمع أبو جهل النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The occasion arose when the preceding verse was revealed; many divine names do not imply many divine beings, unlike worship of distinct entities.
rows.anchor: والكلام رد وتعليم بأن تعدد الأسماء لا يقتضي تعدد المسمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ay is originally interrogative; extra mā makes it conditional, so tadʿū is jussive and the answer begins with fa. The beautiful names permit invocation by any name because the referent is one.
rows.anchor: فإذا اقترنت بها ( ما ) الزائدة أفادت الشرط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Call upon Allah or al-Raḥmān” can mean mention either name in prayer; alternatively, it means name your Lord by either, with the first object omitted.
rows.anchor: ومعنى { ادعوا الله أو ادعوا الرحمن } ادعوا هذا الاسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer-volume instruction connects to the naming command and supports the occasion involving the Prophet's audible invocation of al-Raḥmān.
rows.anchor: بسبب جهر النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في دعائه باسم الرحمن

rows.speaker: السلف
rows.claim: Early authorities explained ṣalāt here as either supplication or formal prayer; those choosing formal prayer mean its recitation, which can be loud or quiet.
rows.anchor: فسرها السلف هنا بالمعنيين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In either interpretation, the Prophet audibly invoked al-Raḥmān; some polytheists asked who it was or accused him of invoking two gods, while others insulted the Qur'an, Messenger, or al-Raḥmān as another lord.
rows.anchor: وعلى كلا الاحتمالين فقد جهر النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بذكر الرحمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opponents may have read public recitation as provocation; excessive loudness could inflame them and harden disbelief when the aim was to soften hearts.
rows.anchor: فأمره الله تعالى بأن لا يجهر بصلاته هذا الجهر تجنبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ban targets excessive loudness; the ban on whispering prevents secret or wholly silent prayer so potential converts can hear it.
rows.anchor: والمقصود من الكلام النهي عن شدة الجهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After forbidding loud prayer to avoid hardening opponents, God commands public affirmation of unity to end confusion that al-Raḥmān is another being, a partner or helper.
rows.anchor: لما كان النهي عن الجهر بالدعاء أو قراءة الصلاة سدا لذريعة زيادة تصميمهم على الكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Praise belongs to God” rhetorically singles Him out as deserving all praise, treating other reasons for praise as negligible beside His.
rows.anchor: وجملة { الحمد لله } تقتضي تخصيصه تعالى بالحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min means “because of” humiliation: need for a supporter arises from incapacity, so God needs none; alternatively walī includes a protector, with min governing that implied meaning.
rows.anchor: و ( من ) في قوله : { من الذل } بمعنى لام التعليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Magnifying God means believing in His necessary existence, absolute independence, and every perfected attribute, whose opposites are deficiencies.
rows.anchor: ومعنى { كبره } اعتقد أنه كبير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The three descriptions explain exclusive praise; the cognate object intensifies magnification, its indefinite form adds grandeur, and only One with these qualities can bestow otherwise impossible blessings.
rows.anchor: والإتيان بالمفعول المطلق بعد { كبره } للتوكيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet called the surah al-Kahf.
rows.anchor: سماها رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم سورة الكهف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslim and Abū Dāwūd report from Abū al-Dardāʾ that memorizing ten opening verses protects from the Dajjāl; Muslim also says ten final verses. Al-Tirmidhī reports three opening verses and grades it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.
rows.anchor: من حفظ عشر آيات من أول سورة الكهف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib's Bukhārī report names the surah: a cloud covered a man reciting it by a tethered horse, which became restless; the Prophet identified it as tranquility descending with the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: وكذلك وردت تسميتها عن البراء بن عازب في ( صحيح البخاري )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report by Ibn Mardawayh says the Prophet called it Sūrat Aṣḥāb al-Kahf.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث أخرجه ابن مردويه عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه سماها

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports consensus that the surah is Meccan. Farqad's report makes 18:1-8 Medinan, but he prefers the Meccan account; proposed Medinan passages at 18:28-29 and 18:107-end are weak.
rows.anchor: وهي مكية بالاتفاق كما حكاه ابن عطية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah followed al-Ghāshiyah and preceded al-Shūrā; Jābir ibn Zayd ranks it sixty-eighth in revelation order.
rows.anchor: نزلت بعد سورة الغاشية وقبل سورة الشورى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its virtue reports vary in strength, with those already cited the soundest; another report says the whole surah descended at once with seventy thousand angels, omitted by al-Suyūṭī from al-Itqān.
rows.anchor: وهي من السور التي نزلت جملة واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse counts differ: Medina and Mecca count 105, Syria 106, Basra 111, and Kufa 110 because they split some verses differently.
rows.anchor: عدت آيها في عدد قراء المدينة ومكة مائة وخمسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purpose phrase attaches to “sent down”; Allah is its subject, while the first object of “warn” is omitted to generalize or stress the punishment and threaten deniers of the Qur'an's divine origin.
rows.anchor: والضمير المرفوع عائد إلى اسم الجلالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-baʾs is painful severity and can mean military force because it hurts enemies. The author prefers worldly suffering here, especially killing and capture by Muslims, decreed by God though enacted by people; ladun has literal and figurative senses.
rows.anchor: والبأس : الشدة في الألم . ويطلق على القوة في الحرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning worldly warning does not make it the book's only purpose; one action may have several causes.
rows.anchor: وليس في جعل الإنذار ببأس الدنيا علة لإنزال الكتاب

rows.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
rows.claim: An alternative takes the warning as afterlife punishment, with “from Him” literal; most exegetes choose this, while Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī include both worldly and afterlife punishments.
rows.anchor: وبهذا الوجه فسر جمهور المفسرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The recipient of warning is omitted because context identifies those rejecting the book and its recipient, contrasted with believers who receive good news.
rows.anchor: وحذف مفعول { ينذر } لدلالة السياق عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Giving believers good news is another reason the book was sent down, coordinated with its warning.
rows.anchor: فهو سبب آخر لإنزال الكتاب أثارته مناسبة ذكر الإنذار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That they have a good reward” is the object of “give good news,” with a preposition omitted; mentioning faith and righteous deeds points to both as grounds for reward.
rows.anchor: بحذف حرف الجر مع ( أن )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an generally does not detail cases combining faith with more or fewer righteous deeds, for which ample evidence exists.
rows.anchor: ولا يتعرض القرآن في الغالب لحالة حصول الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abiding portrays their pleasures as an enveloping place from which they are never parted; “forever” adds enduring duration, not mere repetition.
rows.anchor: شبه ما لهم من اللذات والملائمات بالظرف الذي يستقر فيه حاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warning those claiming God has a child is another purpose of revelation. It differs from 18:2 if that means worldly punishment; if both worlds, repetition emphasizes and identifies this group.
rows.anchor: إنذار مخصوص مقابل لما بشر به المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This warning concerns eternal afterlife punishment; its omitted object is recovered from contrast with good news.
rows.anchor: وهذا إنذار بجزاء خالدين فيه وهو عذاب الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those claiming God has a child here are Meccan polytheists who called angels God's daughters, not Christians calling Jesus God's son, since Meccan revelation had not addressed People of the Book directly.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالذين قالوا اتخذ الله ولدا } هنا المشركون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The relative clause publicizes their notorious claim to condemn it and imply it merits warning alongside other causes.
rows.anchor: والتعبير عنهم بالموصول وصلته لأنهم قد عرفوا بهذه المقالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Walad denotes offspring of either sex and can be singular or plural; this was explained at 10:68.
rows.anchor: والولد : اسم لمن يولد من ذكر أو أنثى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about having no knowledge is circumstantial to “those who said”; its pronoun refers to the claim understood from their saying.
rows.anchor: وجملة ما لهم به من علم } حال من { الذين قالوا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min reinforces negation: they assert a baseless claim, more shamefully, with knowledge standing for proof or its cause, as in 23:117.
rows.anchor: وفائدة ذكر هذه الحال أنها أشنع في كفرهم وهي أن يقولوا كذبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Nor their forefathers” cuts off ancestral imitation as an excuse: if their parents had no proof, descendants have no grounds to follow them.
rows.anchor: وعطف { ولا لآبائهم } لقطع حجتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “How grave a word!” is an independent exclamation; kaburat shifts from physical bigness to severity, and the accusative tamyīz marks astonishment at its heinousness.
rows.anchor: وفعل { كبرت } بضم الباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “it grew grave” refers to the word signaled by the clarifying accusative; kalimah commonly means a full utterance, as in 23:100 and the report quoting Labīd.
rows.anchor: وأطلقت الكلمة على الكلام وهو إطلاق شائع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Coming from their mouths” modifies “word”; its present tense vividly depicts insolence and implies this impossible claim originates in mouths rather than rational minds.
rows.anchor: وجملة تخرج من أفواههم } صفة ل { كلمة }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Afwāh is the plural of fam: original fuwah/fiw lost its hāʾ, wāw became alif, then mīm replaced it because it resembles the original bilabial wāw; the plural restores the root.
rows.anchor: والأفواه : جمع فم وهو بوزن أفعال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They say nothing but lies” confirms that the claim issues from their mouths: speech without correspondence to reality is falsehood, its only quality.
rows.anchor: وجملة { إن يقولون إلا كذبا } مؤكدة لمضمون جملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They say” may refer specifically to claiming God took a child; alternatively, it generalizes to every claim about Qur'an, Islam, or belief opposing Islam, as a concluding restriction.
rows.anchor: خصوص قولهم : { اتخذ الله ولدا ( الكهف : 4 )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse may depict the Prophet's grief at rejection by likening people to loved ones departing while he sees traces of their homes; ʿalā is circumstantial and figuratively expresses attachment to place.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون المعنى تمثيل حال الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spoken near the end of hope for their belief, the verse prepares the Prophet for likely rejection with compassion; the imperfect means if they persist in not believing.
rows.anchor: وكأن هذا الكلام سيق إلى الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم في آخر أوقات رجائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative points to the Qur'an, mentally present; ḥadīth means a report or extended account of newly conveyed news, as discussed at 39:23.
rows.anchor: واسم الإشارة وبيانه مراد به القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asafan is a causal complement to “destroy yourself”: grief is so severe he would kill himself; the conditional interrupts the two complements and needs no separate answer.
rows.anchor: أي قاتلها لأجل شدة الحزن
